findings.text: Participants viewed the online BPA process as an improvement over the earlier fully offline process in terms of convenience, but said the website/software still needs to be more user-friendly.

Repeated technical problems were reported while uploading architectural drawings — DFX/DXF-type files not uploading, applications failing to submit, and system error messages even when the applicant/architect believed the drawings were correct.

Technical difficulty was significant enough that applicants sought help from friends/other technical persons when they could not submit an application; this assistance did not always resolve the issue.

One participant said an application could not be submitted at the user end, while others reported that submitted applications could receive a response relatively quickly, indicating the main bottleneck occurs before successful submission rather than after.

The process involves multiple stakeholders/approvals for a building project — fire, pollution/environment, waste management, lift permission and other linked clearances — creating coordination complexity.
Participants indicated the system is moving toward/has a single-window arrangement, but applicants may still have to deal with requirements or approvals associated with different departments.

Applicants may have to undertake follow-up calls or visits when the digital process does not work; the earlier offline interaction was described as generally smooth/helpful in some cases, especially where staff assisted.
A clear grievance/complaint redressal mechanism was not known to participants; the discussion concluded a proper response mechanism should be available when a query is not resolved.
Architectural/technical capacity is a constraint — only a limited number of architects are comfortable with the relevant software/online approval process.

Land-use classification and restrictions emerged as a policy-level issue — agricultural land cannot simply be used for commercial purposes, and land-use/master-plan restrictions affect building proposals.

Building height restrictions were discussed in the context of the State's conditions, including seismic considerations; participants indicated government-level changes to the existing framework may be under consideration.
A completion-stage inspection by a small team was described — the team visited the site, took photographs and required additional photographs to be submitted.
Physical presence is generally reduced after digitisation, but physical visits/follow-up remain relevant when online submission or other parts of the process do not work.

Payment is linked to the approval process and was discussed as being based on parameters such as area/square feet, made through an online unified payment arrangement via the Government e-GRAS system for the single-window setup.
The sequencing described was approval followed by payment and then issuance of the relevant permission/approval.
The discussion did not establish a clear case of the same document being repeatedly submitted to multiple departments.

Technical failure during drawing upload/submission can prevent an application from moving forward; some early-stage problems were attributed to the newness/bugs in the online system, possibly since fixed.
Improve the BPA website and software so it is more user-friendly and reliably accepts the required architectural drawing formats, with stronger validation/checkpoint features before final submission.
Provide a clear and easily accessible complaint/grievance redressal mechanism with a defined response process.

No clear evidence of unofficial payments or hidden charges was reported; participants specifically stated they had not paid hidden charges in the instances discussed, and some described departmental staff as helpful during office interactions.

gaps.text: ED gives a 10-15 day (up to 30-day) processing timeline for BPA, but FGD participants gave no specific day-count of their own — only that response is 'relatively quick' once successfully submitted — so the ED's specific day-range could not be independently cross-verified by business testimony.

The ED record contains no mention of a grievance/complaint redressal process for BPA at all, but FGD participants explicitly raised its absence as a pain point ('a proper complaint/redressal system should be there') — a gap the ED discussion did not surface.

FGD corroborates the ED's architect-capacity bottleneck finding: both sources independently describe only a small pool of architects able to handle the OBPS-linked drawing software, reinforcing this as a verified bottleneck rather than an isolated official claim.

Neither ED nor FGD specifies an exact BPA fee amount; FGD adds that payment is linked to area/square footage and made via the e-GRAS unified payment system for the single-window setup, but gives no concrete figures.

Both sources reference possible future change to land-use/building-height norms — ED discussed a risk-based classification proposal from officials, while FGD participants separately noted 'government-level changes to the existing framework may be under consideration' — converging on anticipated reform not yet finalized.

findings.text: GST welcome-kit delivery was reported as problematic in some cases because the address was not recognised/matched correctly; affected participants had to approach the GST office and show departmental communication before the matter could be resolved.
Two participants described a similar experience in which an additional/unofficial amount was sought in connection with the welcome-kit/address issue.
The GST application portal was reported to have a location/address selection or matching problem, particularly where detailed address information such as a floor number was entered.
Awareness of the GST complaint process is weak — some participants did not know where or how to complain, and one described difficulty finding a responsive contact and receiving useful guidance.
Users who depend on consultants/CA professionals incur consultation charges; participants noted that users with fewer financial resources may find this additional cost burdensome.
During periods of business shutdown/disruption, participants raised concerns about continuing GST return-filing obligations and associated charges/penalties even with little or no business activity.

One participant obtained GST registration for a government tender but had not received the tender; the discussion raised concern about continuing compliance obligations despite the business opportunity not materialising.
Participants suggested GST compliance should provide a practical relaxation or nil-filing mechanism for periods when a business is genuinely shut down or has no activity.
A policy-level concern was raised about continued GST compliance costs/penalties where registration was obtained for a proposed tender/activity that does not materialise.
Participants implicitly called for a more accessible system for users who cannot afford or do not have access to professional consultants.
Address/location matching on the GST portal can create downstream problems in delivery/verification of the GST welcome kit, sometimes requiring a physical visit to the GST office.
The complaint/redressal process was not sufficiently visible or usable — users were unsure whom to contact, and available contacts did not always provide a solution.
GST filing is often delegated to CAs, consultants or accounts teams; this reduces the burden for some organisations but creates dependence on intermediaries for others.

Registration processing itself was generally viewed positively and faster than before; the principal procedural concerns were around exceptions, address problems, grievance handling and return compliance rather than basic registration speed.
Where GST registration was straightforward, participants reported very quick processing, including same-day or approximately two-hour issuance in some cases.
In problem cases, delay was associated with address/location mismatch and non-delivery of the GST welcome kit, which required a visit to the GST office.

One participant reported a filing/application experience of roughly 3-7 days, while another described an approximately 10-minute completion time for the application itself — variation attributed to user-side preparation and intermediary involvement.
The basic GST registration process has improved materially compared with earlier experiences; several participants described it as quick, simple and well organised.

The experience of informal extra payment was reported only in connection with particular welcome-kit/address cases; the discussion does not establish that such payments are routine across GST registration.

remarks: FGD-only record (Mode B) — Manipur's ED pass did not cover GST Registration; this structured record is derived solely from business testimony and has not been verified against an official source.

Basic registration speed was generally viewed positively by participants; the principal issues raised were about exception handling (address mismatch/welcome kit), grievance redressal, and continuing compliance obligations in specific circumstances (business shutdown, non-materialised tenders).

findings.text: Renewal requires repeated data entry: a participant reported that information and documents already entered in the portal had to be entered again for renewal, described as time-consuming, especially where premises/details had not changed.

Limited reuse of prior online applications: participants suggested the portal should retrieve the previous application and allow users to update only changed information rather than re-entering all details.
Portal usability and guidance gaps: the online portal was new/unfamiliar to some users, and clearer instructions or a step-by-step guide would help.
Difficulty resolving issues without visiting the office: applicants located away from the fire office need to be able to resolve queries remotely.

Multiple branches/units under the same business details: a participant described difficulties when one company has multiple factories or brands sharing company/PAN details, with constraints around repeated entry and the portal/user account.

Risk of mismatch between submitted plans and actual construction: participants raised concern that the building/layout submitted for approval may differ materially from what is ultimately constructed, potentially undermining fire-safety assessment.

Coordination between fire-safety clearance and building approvals: participants discussed whether fire-safety requirements should be linked with building-plan approval and/or occupancy certification so the approved plan and the physical building are aligned.
Need for a clearer approach to pre- and post-construction checks was raised, but the discussion did not establish a final policy position or confirmed change.
Responsibility for deviations from approved plans was debated as a safety/regulatory-coordination concern, not resolved during the meeting.
Participants discussed possible changes to certificate validity and third-party inspection; one speaker advised applicants to follow prevailing state guidelines.

Reported sequence: apply online, undergo a site inspection, receive the certificate after inspection — several comments suggested inspection may occur in approximately 7-10 days, reported in discussion and not an official service standard.
Renewal workflow does not adequately reuse existing records; a previous-application retrieval and update function was proposed.
Participants proposed that a newly introduced portal should include clear guidance explaining how to fill in forms and which requirements apply to different establishment types.
Need for better support for multi-unit applicants, since the workflow may be difficult where the same company operates several factories/branches or holds multiple brands/certificates.
Participants suggested inspection should verify whether the physical site corresponds with the submitted layout, potentially supported by evidence such as photographs.
A participant estimated inspection could take around 7-10 days after submission — a participant-reported estimate, not a verified or prescribed timeline.
Repeated entry of previously submitted details was identified as time-consuming, particularly during renewal.
The mismatch between submitted building plans and the actual constructed site was raised as a risk that could complicate verification and coordination between authorities.
Participants generally described the online application as manageable, and some said they had obtained an electronic certificate.
The meeting did not conclude with a confirmed decision on changes to rules, certificate validity, third-party inspections, or portal integration.

findings.text: Participants described the GST refund process as lengthy, particularly where refunds are subject to verification, scrutiny or risk profiling.
Refund amounts can remain blocked for a considerable period, affecting the ability to rotate working capital in the business.
Participants generally viewed the GST portal as substantially online and easier than earlier processes, but indicated refund settlement time remains the main concern.
Uncertainty exists regarding GST charged on logistics services and whether the related GST can be claimed back as ITC/refund; logistics providers were not uniformly clear on this issue.
Participants suggested the prescribed/standard refund processing period should be reduced so eligible funds return to businesses faster.
A specific suggestion was to reduce the stated 90-day refund period to approximately 45-60 days, preferably through an all-India policy change rather than a state-specific arrangement.
Participants sought clearer policy-level guidance on the treatment/claimability of GST paid on logistics services.
The refund process is largely online, and participants indicated they generally do not need to visit the department unless a notice, query or issue arises.
Where a refund is subjected to risk profiling/audit-type scrutiny of potentially risky/export cases, additional processing time can arise.
Grievance/complaint mechanisms can work when the concerned issue is clearly taken to the department; one participant reported personally approaching the office and receiving assistance.
The overall concern was less about availability of an online portal and more about the time taken after filing/acknowledgement for the refund to be completed.
Risk profiling and scrutiny of refund/export cases were identified as factors that can extend processing time.
Participants referred to a standard processing window after filing/acknowledgement and felt this period should be shortened.
Broader, all-India requirements may constrain a state-only reduction in the refund timeline.
Maintain and strengthen the online GST process and grievance mechanism, as participants generally found the portal convenient and departmental support available when issues were raised.
Where risk-based scrutiny is necessary, keep the process predictable and minimise avoidable waiting time so working capital is not blocked for extended periods.

Participants did not describe the GST refund system in Manipur as fundamentally inaccessible; they viewed it as comparatively smooth and online, with processing time the principal area for improvement.
The working-capital impact of delayed refunds was emphasised; one participant referred to amounts in the range of ₹1-2 crore being potentially significant when blocked in the business.

steps.note: Risk profiling was identified as a factor extending processing time before refund release.

steps.title: Department may raise a notice or query, requiring applicant response/visit
steps.note: Participants indicated they generally do not need to visit the department unless a notice, query or issue arises; grievance redressal was described as effective when the issue is taken directly to the concerned GST office.

steps.title: Refund released/settled
steps.note: Discussed as currently taking around a standard 90-day window; participants proposed reducing this to roughly 45-60 days.

remarks: FGD-only record (Mode B) — Manipur's ED pass did not cover GST Tax Refund; this structured record is derived solely from business testimony and has not been verified against an official source.

Participants did not describe the Manipur GST refund system as fundamentally inaccessible; the online portal and grievance channel were viewed positively, with processing/turnaround time as the principal area for improvement.

A separate, unresolved concern was raised about whether GST paid on logistics services can be claimed back as ITC/refund, with logistics providers reportedly not uniformly clear on the applicable treatment — a cross-cutting ambiguity rather than one specific to Manipur's refund procedure.
